summary: A 1970 note on logical message synchronization in the early network. It deals with keeping messages in step between computers. It is a design discussion, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 58 asks how a receiver can tell where logical messages begin and end when they are carried in physical messages. It explains why a lost bit can make recovery difficult and discusses possible ways to mark boundaries.

questions: what is the logical message synchronization problem
how do you know where messages start and end
what happens if a bit is lost
subtitle: A discussion of how a receiver can find logical message boundaries.

tldr.problem: When logical messages do not align with physical message boundaries, a receiver needs a way to find their starts and ends, especially after a bit is lost.
tldr.mechanism: The note discusses starting logical messages on physical boundaries, or preceding them with a bit count or data-type specification.
tldr.outcome: The author raises the synchronization problem and its tradeoffs without recommending a final solution.

today: The unit metadata records RFC 58 as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The note raises message synchronization as a design question and does not select a final solution.

sections.title: Logical and Physical Messages
sections.content:
The note distinguishes logical messages from physical messages. It discusses whether a logical message should begin at a physical-message boundary, while pointing out that this alone does not identify where the logical message ends.

A bit count or data-type specification before each logical message is raised as a possible way to mark its structure.
sections.plainLanguage: A logical message may not match the boundaries of the physical messages carrying it. The receiver needs information that shows where the logical message ends as well as where it begins.

sections.title: Why a Lost Bit Breaks Synchronization
sections.content:
If a bit is dropped, the receiver may no longer know where a logical message begins. The note says one possible recovery method is to shift through the incoming bits and look for a plausible message, but this could take time and produce false synchronization.

Another possible response is to stop sending, clear waiting input and resume when the hosts are synchronized. The author notes that buffering in the network and at both hosts makes it hard to know whether all pending data has arrived.
sections.plainLanguage: After a bit is lost, the receiver may not know where to look for the next message. Searching through the data can be slow and may mistake ordinary data for a boundary.

sections.title: A Boundary-Based Option
sections.content:
The note describes retaining the restriction that each logical message starts at a physical-message boundary. The receiver could then check the start of each physical message for a logical-message header, rather than searching the whole input stream.

The author does not propose this as a settled solution. He says the issue should be faced early if the restriction is chosen.
sections.plainLanguage: Starting every logical message at a physical boundary could make recovery faster and safer. The author raises this as an option, not a final decision.
